He cited a similar drone strike on a Ukraine-Moldova crossing, and said the CIA reports warn of “possible events” on the eastern flank. by Kyiv Post | Sept. 10, 2026, 10:48 pm Flip Share Facebook X (Twitter) LinkedIn Bluesky Email Copy Copied Polish Prime Minister Donald Tusk speaks during a press conference at the Artus Court during the Eastern Flank Summit, in Gdansk, Poland, on June 25, 2026. (Photo by Wojtek RADWANSKI / AFP) Content Share Facebook X (Twitter) LinkedIn Bluesky Email Copy Copied Flip Poland believes Russia may target its border crossings with Ukraine, after Warsaw averted a threat to one of its own crossings overnight. Polish Prime Minister Donald Tusk made the remarks at a press conference in Bratislava, Slovakia on Thursday, Sept. 10, according to Reuters . Overnight from Tuesday into Wednesday, Sept. 8-9, Russian drones struck the Ukrainian side of the Tudora-Starokozache crossing , killing two Ukrainian nationals and injuring seven people, including a Moldovan national. JOIN US ON TELEGRAM Follow our coverage of the war on the @Kyivpost_official . “Last night, thanks to cooperation between our services and their ​Ukrainian counterparts, a direct threat to one of the border crossings ​was averted,” Tusk said. “As you know, Russia has already resorted to provocative attacks on border ​crossings – for instance, in Moldova. We expect similar actions targeting ​border crossings with Ukraine in other countries, including Poland,” he continued. Advertisement Tusk cites CIA warning Tusk said he had also received what he described as “a fairly precise report directly from the CIA regarding possible events in the coming months,” which he said matched warnings he had issued for months about Russian provocations. He also urged Poland and the rest of Europe to prepare for a range of scenarios, not only along the Ukrainian front but also across the eastern flank, echoing his previous warnings that Russia may attack NATO. Moldova crossing struck two days earlier On Wednesday, Moldova accused Russia of deliberately Tudora-Starokozache border crossing and using false claims about weapons shipments to Ukraine to justify the strike and civilian deaths. Other Topics of Interest Zelensky Says He Plans to Meet Trump in New York in Late September Zelensky plans talks with Trump in New York as diplomatic efforts continue and Canada’s Carney confirms recent discussions with the US president on Ukraine. Russia’s defense ministry confirmed the attack, saying Moscow had struck logistic facilities that were allegedly being used to transport military cargo to Ukraine. The incident followed a series of Russian attacks on Moldovan-Ukrainian crossings in August. Moldovan President Maia Sandu accused Russia of deliberately sending some of the drones into Moldova’s airspace . “Judging by the trajectory of those drones, we can say which are sent intentionally and which are there by chance,” Sandu said, adding that in both cases, the drones violate the country’s airspace, Sandu said on Aug. 17. Advertisement “And the only one who is guilty, the only party that is guilty of these things, is the Russian Federation, which started this war,” she continued. Poland sees little hope for recent Ukraine peace talks Tomasz Siemoniak, Poland’s minister overseeing the country’s special services, has met with CIA Director John Ratcliffe over fears that Russia may attack NATO. Siemoniak confirmed the meeting with Ratcliffe on Tuesday, which was held at the agency’s headquarters near Washington. Ratcliffe had traveled to Moscow on Aug. 25, in his first visit to Russia during his tenure in the agency, where he held talks with Sergei Naryshkin, head of Russia’s Foreign Intelligence Service (SVR), and Alexander Bortnikov, director of the Federal Security Service (FSB). Although further details of the talks were not made publicly known, Politico reported on Aug. 26 that Ratcliffe warned Putin against attacking a NATO member , with the discussion centering on the Baltic states – Estonia, Latvia and Lithuania. Putin was reportedly also warned against providing military and economic support to Iran, which Moscow views as an ally and has received Shahed drones from. Advertisement US President Donald Trump dismissed the possibility of Russia attacking NATO on Aug. 27, while rejecting reports that Ratcliffe traveled to Moscow to warn the Kremlin against such a move. Separately, he downplayed the visit by calling it “semi-routine,” before saying that his administration was “working very hard to get that war ended.” On Sunday, Sept. 6, senior US envoys Steve Witkoff and Jared Kushner visited Kyiv for the first time as Washington’s intermediaries, where where they held bilateral talks with President Volodymyr Zelensky and the American emissaries , followed by a multilateral session that included national security advisers from the UK, France, and Germany. The two also traveled to Moscow and held more than three hours of talks with Russian President Vladimir Putin on Saturday evening, Sept. 5, subsequently having an informal working dinner. Despite the weekend meetings being described as substantial and productive, and despite the Kremlin signaling openness for further trilateral talks , Russia continues to conduct large-scale attacks on Ukraine, with the latest attacks killing seven and injuring at least 118 nationwide on Thursday. Polish Foreign Minister Radosław Sikorski, speaking in Latvia on Wednesday, said he was not optimistic regarding the prospect of peace negotiations, adding that Moscow has not softened its military aims and continues to reject ceasefire proposals . Ukraine: Russian drone barrage on Kyiv kills teenage boy and wounds 20 residents Copy/paste the link below: Copy Copy/paste the article video embed link below: Copy Updated: 25/09/2026 - 15:50 GMT+2 A 14-year-old boy was killed after a Russian drone tore into a 16-storey apartment block in Kyiv’s Pecherskyi district overnight on Friday 25 September 2026. … More The aircraft struck between the 10th and 11th floors during a barrage that followed air-raid warnings in the Ukrainian capital. At least seven people were initially injured**,** including a nine-year-old boy , as rescue teams evacuated residents and worked through broken glass and debris. ADVERTISEMENT ADVERTISEMENT As attacks continued, the number of injured across Kyiv climbed to 20 , including eight people taken to hospital. Buildings were also damaged in Podilskyi and Solomianskyi, while another drone later struck a five-storey non-residential property in Shevchenkivskyi. The latest assault came after ballistic missiles killed two people and injured eight in Kyiv the previous night. President Volodymyr Zelenskyy said eight regions came under Russian attack. Ukraine reported 282 attack drones as well as several types of missile launched overnight. Odesa was also hit, leaving one person dead and another injured . Russia said it targeted Ukrainian defence and logistics facilities and denies deliberately attacking civilians, while Russian authorities reported casualties from Ukrainian long-range strikes. Photograph: Christopher Thomond/The Guardian The Archers BBC to stop recording The Archers in Birmingham for first time in its 75-year history Plans for a new theatre for world’s longest-running soap in Digbeth scrapped as part of cost-cutting measures Michael Savage Media editor Mon 12 Oct 2026 15.56 EDT Last modified on Mon 12 Oct 2026 16.52 EDT Share Prefer the Guardian on Google The BBC is set to stop recording The Archers in Birmingham for the first time in the show’s 75-year history, after scrapping plans for a radio drama theatre that was to be the new home of the world’s longest-running soap opera. A pledge to move recordings to the so-called Tea Factory, the BBC’s new Birmingham hub in Digbeth, has become the latest victim of the corporation’s £500m cuts plan . While the soap’s production team are still scheduled to make the move, the BBC is now looking to record it at an existing UK studio. It will also consider private studios in the West Midlands , but BBC insiders are already concerned that ending its Birmingham-based recordings and separating the actors from the production crew will have an impact on the show. Production staff regularly engage with the actors at the last minute to tweak scripts and storylines, raising concerns that their being in different places will stifle creativity. “It is going to weaken the show,” said a source. “It will change the DNA of the show.” BBC axes long-running Radio 4 show You and Yours in push towards podcasts Read more Moving the recording of The Archers from the BBC’s existing Birmingham base, The Mailbox, to the Tea Factory was due to take place in 2028. In an email to staff last week, a BBC executive said: “After careful consideration and as part of the BBC’s wider drive to reduce costs, the decision has been made … to not build a new radio drama studio for The Archers in the Tea Factory in Digbeth. “Consequently, options are being explored to identify suitable studio facilities where The Archers will be recorded. That currently includes looking into potential opportunities in the West Midlands, as well as across other parts of the UK. “To be clear, no decision has yet been reached. The priority is to find the most cost-effective solution which will maintain The Archers’ high production standards in addition to delivering significant savings. “The Archers is a jewel in the BBC’s crown. It’s been going for an incomparable 75 years – as has its connection with the West Midlands. It remains a hugely vital part of our future.” The show has been associated with Birmingham since it started in 1951. Sources said it remained part of the cultural fabric of the city, and the show employs local writers and freelancers. However, others said the show’s recording schedule meant actors were only in the studio for about eight days a month, while many of the cast live across the UK. skip past newsletter promotion Free newsletter | Every weekday Sign up to First Edition Our morning email breaks down the key stories of the day, telling you what’s happening and why it matters after newsletter promotion Some now fear recordings will default to London and that the show’s staff will eventually follow. However, the BBC has been clear that production staff will move to the new Birmingham headquarters as planned. It is not clear whether Lisa Nandy, the culture secretary, was aware of the plans. Boosting BBC production outside London has regularly been at the top of her agenda. It is a sign that even some of the BBC’s most revered titles are being affected by cuts, with more announcements expected in the coming days. Matt Brittin, the BBC’s director general, has already faced anger from staff who believe more of the corporation’s manager class should be targeted instead. BBC morale dented by gradual ‘bloodletting’ after weeks of job cuts Read more A BBC spokesperson said: “We recognise and value The Archers’ longstanding relationship with the West Midlands, which remains an important part of the programme’s future, and The Archers production team will remain in their current home in the Mailbox and move, as planned, to the Tea Factory in Digbeth in early 2028. “However, after careful consideration, as part of the BBC’s wider drive to reduce costs, we are no longer building a new recording studio for The Archers in the Tea Factory. “We’re currently assessing the BBC’s existing studio facilities around the UK as well as other external studio options in the West Midlands to find a more cost-effective solution.” Explore more on these topics The Archers Birmingham Radio drama West Midlands Soap opera Radio Public service broadcasting news Share Reuse this content More on this story More on this story BBC axes long-running Radio 4 show You and Yours in push towards podcasts BBC boss faces barrage of staff criticism over job cuts in junior ranks BBC morale dented by gradual ‘bloodletting’ after weeks of job cuts BBC ‘risks entering inescapable doom spiral’ as further cuts hit TV and radio BBC to axe sports bulletins on its TV news channel BBC cash reserves hit lowest level in a decade after big single-year spend BBC boss concedes real prospect of strikes over pay and job cuts ‘What has the BBC ever done for me?’ Romesh Ranganathan reboots corporation’s 1985 licence fee plea BBC staff fear strike action inevitable after anger at 1% pay rise offer BBC News braces for major round of job cuts in broadcaster’s £500m cost-saving drive Most viewed Most viewed Film Books Music Art & design TV & radio Stage Classical Games Design a better world

Illustration: Guardian Design View image in fullscreen The company pulled the plug on the cruise after it said monthly fuel costs per cabin had gone from $1,800 to as much as $8,000. Illustration: Guardian Design The Saturday read Cruises The cursed cruise: how the dream of never-ending luxury at sea became a nightmare The MV Odyssey was billed as the ultimate escape from Donald Trump. Instead, the oil shock caused by his war has left passengers unceremoniously dumped in Cambodia Oliver Holmes in Bangkok, Daniel Boffey in London and Adeshola Ore in Melbourne Fri 30 Oct 2026 23.00 EDT Last modified on Fri 30 Oct 2026 23.02 EDT Share The idea was a never-ending retirement at sea, a continuous voyage around the globe. The promise to the passengers of the MV Odyssey cruise ship – many approaching the autumn of their lives – was that on the open seas they could cut loose from the troubles of the world. But the world had other ideas. The end came in an announcement as stark as it was brief: they had seven hours to get off. They were going no further than Cambodia . The Odyssey, owned by Florida-based Villa Vie Residences, had first set sail from Belfast, Northern Ireland, in October 2024 with an explicit offer: Donald Trump had been re-elected to the White House, and this was a way for those ill-disposed to the president to enjoy a four-year “skip forward”. View image in fullscreen Passengers disembark from the Odyssey at Sihanoukville port in Cambodia. Photograph: Kith Serey/EPA For $319,998, a couple seeking such an escape could head off to the high seas for the length of a presidential term and come back from their journey to nowhere when the danger had passed – or not. For those who had simply had enough, there was a permanent residency option for a few hundred thousand more. Depending on the package, there were also monthly fees on top, which covered food, drinks, wifi, wellness programmes and room cleaning. They would have access to a pool, a pickleball court, a theatre, several bars and a gym. Exotic port destinations would be visited along the way. It was by no means cheap – but the Odyssey was quite accurately billed as the “affordable” option for those interested in such a cocoon. The pioneer in the world of “residential ships”, a vessel called MS The World, offered apartments that typically ranged from $2m to $15m, with the pampered passengers getting to choose where it would go. For that experience, there was a waiting list. The Odyssey was not in that league. Rather than built as a residential ship, it had previously been a traditional cruise liner named MS Braemar. Under that name, it had been turned away from several ports in the Caribbean during the pandemic when its passengers became ill. Cuba finally allowed it to dock, but the vessel never went into service as MS Braemar again. It was sold off by Fred Olsen cruises and adapted by its new owners. Villa Vie described the three-decade-old restructured vessel as “an intimate residential cruise ship offering a new way to live”. View image in fullscreen Passengers onboard the then-MS Braemar wait to disembark in Mariel, Cuba, in March 2020. Photograph: Adalberto Roque/AFP/Getty Images At 642ft (196 metres) long, it was a relatively small ship, but at such prices, and with the world being held firmly at bay, what could go wrong? Neither the more than 200 passengers on the Odyssey nor its cruise operator foresaw the consequences of Trump’s war in Iran. The reality was, there was no escaping the US president. On Tuesday, Villa Vie Residences issued a statement. It had run out of money owing to the soaring price of oil. Monthly fuel costs per cabin in parts of Asia had risen to as much as $8,000 from $1,800, placing it “under unsustainable financial pressure”, it announced. graphic “Since the conflict began in late February, we have taken significant steps to reduce fuel consumption, including slowing the itinerary and spending more time in port,” the company said, explaining the slow death of its business model. “Those measures have not been enough to offset the extraordinary increase in fuel costs, and we have been unable to continue carrying the resulting operating losses.” View image in fullscreen The Villa Vie Odyssey cruise ship leaves Belfast. Photograph: Liam McBurney/PA The Odyssey’s passengers were told to pack up their belongings before being transported on buses into the Cambodian port city of Sihanoukville on the Gulf of Thailand. “We are working with residents to coordinate disembarkation and temporary living arrangements, and are supporting residents, crew, and employees as we evaluate restructuring and recapitalisation alternatives over the next 60 days,” the company said. Map graphic “People were shell-shocked, numb, crying,” said one passenger, Kit Cassingham from the US, who spent two years on the ship with her husband, Randy. They had made their cabin into a home, putting down their own rugs and pictures on the wall. “People were angry. They were hysterical. They were sad … Disbelief,” she added. “I mean, that whole gamut of, what is it, the five stages of grief.” Most of the passengers on the Odyssey were Americans, travelling with an international group of 156 crew members, including a ship’s doctor and two nurses. Many of the passengers were retired or digital nomads. One woman, Holly Hennessy, had been living happily with her cat, Captain, since the ship set sail two years ago. View image in fullscreen Holly Hennessy with her Siamese cat, Captain, in Belfast. Photograph: Liam McBurney/PA One couple, Lanette Canen and Johan Bodin, who said they had bought a cabin with a 15-year guarantee, had been documenting their life at sea on YouTube , including the lead-up to the fateful announcement. The signs of financial distress had been apparent for weeks, they said. “I’m Mr Super Positive, and I’ve felt really drained the last two months,” Bodin recounted in a video. Footage from inside the ship’s lounge on the final night showed residents drinking, as rumours spread that their voyage might be over. Cruise ship staff had requested each passenger contribute $1,800 to ensure the ship had funds to travel to Bangkok. The next day, the couple posted an update showing the inside of their cabin as a voice on the loudspeaker said the ship’s operator had “unfortunately” been “unable to secure the fuel necessary to continue operations”. An email was sent requesting that everyone disembark by 2pm. “We knew the worst-case scenarios, but we didn’t think it would come to reality, which it did,” said Rina Cavazza, a pilates instructor from Brisbane, Australia. View image in fullscreen Rina Cavazza’s cabin on the Villa Vie Odyssey. Photograph: supplied Another passenger, Sherrie Cornett, wrote on Facebook that they were “dropped unceremoniously in the middle of town, left to our own devices”. The company has not provided financial aid, passengers said, or even supplied a list of hotels in Cambodia. It later offered tickets for a charter flight to the US, although many passengers had already left. The company has been contacted for comment. Kit and Randy Cassingham, now in a hotel in Cambodia, reflected on how life changed on the ship once the Iran war began, with ominous signs that the company was running out of money. The food quality began to deteriorate, and there was less of it; there were fewer excursions on shore, they said. View image in fullscreen Randy and Kit Cassingham: ‘Live life while you can because you don’t know how the adventure will turn out.’ Photograph: Tang Chhin Sothy/AFP/Getty Images “I realised as soon as the strait of Hormuz incident came along, the energy of the ship changed,” Kit said. “I think it was because the ship management realised how much more this was going to cost. And then they were starting to do cutbacks that we weren’t aware of yet.” Far from being a haven, the ship became a microcosm for the global economic turmoil. “I watched the world, and I don’t even pay attention to the news, but I’ve watched it just kind of crumble and shatter,” said Kit. “And I’m thinking, ‘it’s going to be difficult no matter what’.” Randy said the writing had long been on the wall. They were, after all, on a ship that “drinks petrol by the metric tonne”. “You know, literally they’re buying 150 metric tonnes of fuel at a time,” he said. “We’re talking about $800,000 if we tried to get a full tank.” While docked in Singapore in August, passengers had already been told the company did not have enough money to continue cruising, and several of the residents had contributed their own funds to get it moving again. “Very few expect to get any money back because we know that they [the company] have been in terrible money problems from the beginning,” said Randy. Passengers had also passed a jar around for money for the crew, who are also stuck in Cambodia, he said. Will the story of the Odyssey put people off cruises? It is unlikely, said Prof Andrew Coggins, an industry analyst, who pointed to an unprecedented boom since the end of the Covid pandemic, with global passengers reaching a historical high of 37.2 million in 2025. Those numbers were in part because of “pent up demand” from those who had been unable to enjoy a cruise during the pandemic years, he said. But it was also the case, he said, that a cruise could offer good value for money. “You get to be pampered, you pack and unpack once, but you see different places, you eat better food than you would get at home, and then you have the romance of going to sea,” he said. View image in fullscreen Going nowhere: the Villa Vie Odyssey at Sihanoukville port in Cambodia. Photograph: Kith Serey/EPA Residential ships such as the Odyssey were, though, in a very small category of their own, Coggins added. “The World is the only other one I know about and I think there are a couple that are trying to start up,” he said. But the finances are notoriously difficult. In 2023, a three-year cruise offered by Miray Cruises , with fares starting at $30,000 per person per year, including accommodation, food, drinks, laundry and even health care, was cancelled weeks before its due departure date owing to an inability to make the sums add up.. To survive choppy world markets, charges to the passengers have to be high, necessitating a concomitant level of luxury. “The World was actually built as a residential ship,” Coggins said. “The cabins or the state rooms are much bigger.” Speaking earlier in the week, Mikael Petterson, who launched Villa Vie Residences in 2023, accepted that he was the “villain in the story” but said he was doing everything he could to help the stranded passengers. “Nobody that’s tried residential cruising has succeeded and we have gone further than anyone else,” he said. “But I think we would have been absolutely fine and we would have seen this through, if there was no Iran war.” Back in Cambodia, Randy has been blogging to keep people updated while they work out what to do next. But he isn’t bitter. For all the promises, he said, all good things must come to an end. “Our message is that we’re not saying ‘poor me’. We know that people are having trouble, that they’re trying to put fuel in their cars, food in their mouths. And we’re very lucky. We’re not crying in our soup. So we are completely aware that we’re very lucky and that we’re going to land on our feet and be OK.” Kit, a transformation coach, agreed. “This isn’t a pity party for us,” she said. “We actually want to say to people: ‘Live your dreams. Go for the gusto. Live life while you can because you don’t know how the adventure will turn out’.” Explore more on these topics Cruises The Saturday read Shipping industry Donald Trump Cambodia Water transport Share Most viewed Most viewed
